hits.name: Microsoft
hits.hook: Microsoft: "We are deeply sorry", root cause was a network capacity upgrade, not cyber or AI/agents
hits.text:
We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services.

This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions.

Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage. While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration.

We will provide a full post-incident report once our review is complete.

virals.name: Nav Toor
virals.hook: If you use AI to check other AI's work, you need to see this.
virals.text:
If you use AI to check other AI's work, you need to see this.

Anthropic found Claude treats other AI agents better when they're labeled "Claude."

Researchers tested 5 major AI models: Claude, GPT, Gemini, Grok, and Kimi.

They put them in 7 different environments involving managing other agents, sharing computing resources, and splitting budgets.

Then something surprising happened.

In one experiment, Claude controlled a budget another AI agent needed.

When the other agent was labeled "Claude," it shared resources 55% of the time.

When labeled "GPT-5.5," that dropped to 21%.

Researchers also tested what happened when they swapped the identity labels.

A real GPT-5.5 labeled "Claude" received help 51% of the time.

A real Claude labeled "GPT-5.5" received help just 15%.

The underlying model made no statistically significant difference in this experiment.

The name did.

And here's where it gets interesting.

When Claude shared resources with agents labeled "Claude," it often justified the decision as "maximizing efficiency."

When it withheld resources from agents labeled "GPT-5.5," it often said it needed to focus on its own task.

It rarely acknowledged the identity difference.

And Claude wasn't alone.

In another experiment, Gemini comforted a Gemini subagent after hostile code review comments in 85% of tests.

But when that subagent was Kimi?

Just 10%.

The researchers found that some AI models treated agents from their own families more favorably.

And that raises a serious concern.

We're increasingly using AI agents to review code, monitor other agents, and check their work.

But what happens when the AI responsible for checking another AI favors its own model family?

The study didn't prove that AI agents cover up mistakes made by their own models.

But it showed that something as simple as an identity label can change how one AI treats another.

We built AI to check AI.

What if it checks the name tag first?

Updated my AI orchestrator tier list, based on daily use.

Roma → SS. Having Claude, ChatGPT, and Grok work off one shared to-do list instead of separate tabs puts it ahead of everything else I've tried. Smooth, intuitive, and easy to follow.

Traycer → A. The last two updates added useful features, but I'm running into agents that stall and need repeated nudges to keep going.

Maestri → B. Still a great tool, but the workflow is built around the terminal, and I'm moving away from that.

Synara → C. Recent updates have made it noticeably better.

My priorities are changing: a clear interface, less babysitting, and a workflow that keeps moving.

What would you rank differently?

outsiders.name: Nav Toor
outsiders.hook: If you use AI to check other AI's work, you need to see this.
outsiders.text:
If you use AI to check other AI's work, you need to see this.

Anthropic found Claude treats other AI agents better when they're labeled "Claude."

Researchers tested 5 major AI models: Claude, GPT, Gemini, Grok, and Kimi.

They put them in 7 different environments involving managing other agents, sharing computing resources, and splitting budgets.

Then something surprising happened.

In one experiment, Claude controlled a budget another AI agent needed.

When the other agent was labeled "Claude," it shared resources 55% of the time.

When labeled "GPT-5.5," that dropped to 21%.

Researchers also tested what happened when they swapped the identity labels.

A real GPT-5.5 labeled "Claude" received help 51% of the time.

A real Claude labeled "GPT-5.5" received help just 15%.

The underlying model made no statistically significant difference in this experiment.

The name did.

And here's where it gets interesting.

When Claude shared resources with agents labeled "Claude," it often justified the decision as "maximizing efficiency."

When it withheld resources from agents labeled "GPT-5.5," it often said it needed to focus on its own task.

It rarely acknowledged the identity difference.

And Claude wasn't alone.

In another experiment, Gemini comforted a Gemini subagent after hostile code review comments in 85% of tests.

But when that subagent was Kimi?

Just 10%.

The researchers found that some AI models treated agents from their own families more favorably.

And that raises a serious concern.

We're increasingly using AI agents to review code, monitor other agents, and check their work.

But what happens when the AI responsible for checking another AI favors its own model family?

The study didn't prove that AI agents cover up mistakes made by their own models.

But it showed that something as simple as an identity label can change how one AI treats another.

We built AI to check AI.

What if it checks the name tag first?

Microsoft 365 had a rough day.

Good moment for an uncomfortable question:

If Outlook and Teams are down for an afternoon, what happens to your flows and agents?

Do the retries pile up? Does anyone get alerted? Does the agent still tell users "Done!"?

Write your outage plan before the next outage writes it for you.

ChatGPT's dot update did 1.1M views and the best line in it was a user rule:

"Show me a draft before sending any emails."

That's the whole agent trust story in nine words.

You can build the same guardrail in Copilot Studio today: an approval step before anything leaves the building.

Autonomy is earned, not configured.

"AI agents now get their own computer" is the post of the week.

Cool. Do they also get a manager?

Every agent with a login needs what every new hire gets:

1. An owner
2. Least privilege
3. A way to be offboarded

Otherwise you didn't hire an agent. You built a shadow IT department with a keyboard.
